lesson.title: A Different Kind of Colony Takes Shape
lesson.summary: North of Virginia, English colonists built settlements driven as much by religious purpose as by profit, producing a New England society organized around towns, churches, and diversified trade rather than a single cash crop.
lesson.body:
By the time English colonization pushed north of the Chesapeake, two contrasting models had already emerged for how an English colony might work. Jamestown had shown that a colony could survive on a single profitable export, tobacco, cultivated by a labor force increasingly organized around indentured servitude and, later, enslaved Africans. The colonies that would form New England, beginning with the Plymouth colony founded by English Separatists in 1620 and expanding dramatically with the Massachusetts Bay Colony after 1630, developed along a genuinely different path, one shaped as much by religious conviction as by commercial ambition.

Geography forced much of this difference. New England's rocky, thin soil and short growing season made large scale cash crop agriculture impractical in the way tobacco worked in Virginia. Colonists instead built a more diversified economy around fishing the rich waters off the coast, shipbuilding using the region's abundant timber, and trade, both with England and, increasingly, with other colonies and the Caribbean. This economic mix meant New England never developed the large plantation estates that came to define the Chesapeake and later the Deep South.

Religion shaped New England's social structure just as powerfully as geography shaped its economy. Many settlers came as Puritans or Separatists seeking to practice their faith without interference from the Church of England, and they organized their communities accordingly. Settlement proceeded through organized towns rather than scattered individual farms, with a meetinghouse and congregation at the center of community life, and colonial governments closely intertwined religious and civic authority in ways that distinguished New England from the more secular, profit driven governance of Virginia.

This religious motivation also produced an unusually strong emphasis on education and literacy, since Puritans believed individuals needed to read scripture directly. Massachusetts Bay founded Harvard College in 1636, remarkably early in the colony's history, to train ministers, and the colony's 1647 law sometimes called the Old Deluder Satan Act required towns of a certain size to establish schools, one of the earliest public education mandates in English America.

The pattern of who migrated also set New England apart from Virginia. Where the Chesapeake colonies drew mostly young, single men working as indentured servants, New England attracted whole families and entire congregations migrating together, producing a more balanced population, lower mortality, and rapid natural population growth rather than a colony that depended on constant fresh immigration simply to maintain its numbers. The chapters that follow on Puritan migration and the Massachusetts Bay Colony specifically will trace how these religious and demographic patterns played out in the founding and governance of New England's most influential colony.
